I went hiking again last weekend. It was pouring rain, but the moment I reached the summit, the sky cleared up. It felt amazing, and the sunshine helped dry my soaked clothes too. That said, I hadn’t slept at all the night before, so I wasn’t feeling very well.

The reason I hadn’t slept was because I was working on something called “Breakout Health.”

I  hear people say that breakouts have been working well lately or that they’ve been failing, but I realized that I had been judging that only based on the stocks I personally watch. So I started wondering what it would look like if I actually quantified it.

Breakout Health is a score based on how stocks that had a 2nd-Pivot Break within the past 20 trading days performed after breaking their pivots.

More specifically, I assign points based on things like whether the stock avoided reaching -1R (=ADR%) within 3 days, whether it reached +1R within 5 days, whether it reached +2R within 10 days, and whether it was still above the pivot 5 days after the breakout. I then calculate a weighted average of those results to create the score.

I’m still testing it as a beta, so I wouldn’t call it finished yet, but I’m going to keep watching it for a while.

The current score is lower than I expected, so I actually think this is a good time to test it.

This is not a predictive indicator. It’s an indicator of current breakout health, so it might be worth keeping in the back of your mind when looking at the market.

If you are in first few years of trading, take the time to *intentionally* journal

Back when I started, I used to think the trading journal was for recording what happened. It is actually for sitting with it until your ‘leaks’ have a name

I would use my journal for recording what happened. Entry, exit, green or red, then close the book and feel like I had done the work. What I was missing is that the useful part starts after the fill is written down, when you stay with the page long enough that the same mistakes jump at you like a pattern. Once you diagnose it, you finally have something to work on.

Most newer traders I talk to have a trade log. Very few have sat with last month’s pages until a pattern was obvious: the skips that were based on fear, the adds that came from pride, the leftover revenge emotions from yesterday they felt obligated to act on the next day. 

You cannot fix a leak you keep describing as “just a bad day.” The journal is where it stops being a generic one-liner of your trading day and starts being a place where you can actually see your weaknesses.

I still mess this up when I am tired and I want my review to be a few lines. But I know for a fact, the weeks I get better at recognizing my mistakes are the ones where I do not leave the page until I can say, in one sentence, what I actually did. Then, the next time it shows up I recognize it realtime in the session instead of in the recap to follow

I recommend intentional trade journaling to any trader, especially if you are in your first few years. It will slowly cut out those annoying hidden patterns you keep falling into that hold yourself back.
